label: app:thm:upper
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{app:thm:upper}
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite rectangular box with open boundary conditions in
fixed dimension $\nu\ge1$, and let
\begin{align}
 H=\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda:\ 1\le|Z|\le k\\
                    \operatorname{diam}(Z)\le r_0}}h_Z,
 \qquad h_Z=h_Z^\dagger,
 \qquad \max_{i\in\Lambda}\sum_{Z\ni i}\|h_Z\|\le1.
 \label{app:eq:local-assumptions}
\end{align}
The on-site dimension is at most $d_0$, and $\nu,d_0,k,r_0$ are fixed.
Assume that $H$ has a unique normalized ground state $\Omega$, energy $E_0$,
and gap $\Delta>0$. Fix a planar cut $L|R$ with cross-section $\mathcal A$.
There are constants $C,C_*$, independent of $|\Lambda|,\mathcal A,
\epsilon,\Delta$, such that for every $0<\epsilon\le1/4$ there exist
$K=K^\dagger$ and a normalized state $\Omega_K$ satisfying
\begin{align}
 K|\Omega_K\rangle&=|\Omega_K\rangle,&
 \|\Omega-\Omega_K\|&\le\delta_K,&
 \|K(1-|\Omega_K\rangle\langle\Omega_K|)\|&\le\epsilon_K,
 \label{app:eq:agsp-definition}\\
 \delta_K+\epsilon_K&\le\epsilon,&
 \operatorname{SR}(K)&\le D_K,&
 \log D_K&\le
 C\left[\mathcal A+
 \left(\frac{\mathcal A L_\epsilon}{\sqrt{\Delta_*}}\right)^{2/3}\right]
 \log^2\!\left(\frac{C_*\mathcal A L_\epsilon}{\Delta_*}\right).
 \label{app:eq:upper-theorem}
\end{align}
In particular, $\|K-|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|\|\le\epsilon$.
Neither frustration freeness nor a local-gap assumption is required.
head: environment
name: AGSP upper bound

label: app:thm:lower
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{app:thm:lower}
There are fixed constants $d_0\le6$, $k\le5$, $r_0\le2$, $\Delta_0>0$,
and $C>0$ with the following properties. For every $m\ge3$, every fixed
$\nu\ge2$, and every rectangular $(\nu-1)$-dimensional cross-section
$\Sigma$ of size $M\ge1$, there is a Hamiltonian satisfying
\eqref{app:eq:local-assumptions} on
\begin{align}
 \Lambda=\{-16m,\ldots,16m\}\times\Sigma,
 \qquad n=M(32m+1),\qquad \mathcal A=M.
 \label{app:eq:lower-geometry}
\end{align}
The cut lies between $x=0$ and $x=1$. The ground state
$\Omega_{M,m}^{(\nu)}$ is unique, the full-system gap is at least
$\Delta_0$, and a product root $o$ obeys
$|\langle o|\Omega_{M,m}^{(\nu)}\rangle|^2\ge1/2$.
There is a fixed projection $P_F=P_L\otimes I_R$, independent of any
approximating state, such that, with
$w_{M,m}:=\|P_F\Omega_{M,m}^{(\nu)}\|^2$,
\begin{align}
 w_{M,m}&\ge
 \exp\!\left[-C\left(M+\sqrt M\,m^{3/2}\right)\right],
 \label{app:eq:target-theorem}\\
 (\mathcal V_L\otimes\mathcal V_R)
 \frac{P_F|\Omega_{M,m}^{(\nu)}\rangle}{\sqrt{w_{M,m}}}
 &=|\Phi\rangle^{\otimes Mm}\otimes|\Xi\rangle,
 \qquad \|\Xi\|=1,
 \label{app:eq:bell-theorem}
\end{align}
where $\mathcal V_L,\mathcal V_R$ are isometries and
$\Phi=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
For every integer $1\le D\le2^{Mm}$,
\begin{align}
 \inf_{\operatorname{SR}(\phi)\le D}
 \|\Omega_{M,m}^{(\nu)}-\phi\|^2
 \ge w_{M,m}\left(1-\frac{D}{2^{Mm}}\right).
 \label{app:eq:finite-tail-theorem}
\end{align}
The approximating vector $\phi$ need not be normalized.
In one dimension there is a nearest-neighbor, two-body construction on
$n=32m$ sites, with $\mathcal A=1$, the same constant-gap and root-overlap
properties, and a fixed projection extracting $m$ Bell pairs with
$w_m\ge e^{-Cm^{3/2}}$.

label: app:lem:moment
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Exponential energy moment

label: app:eq:microscopic-commutator
title: Proof
body_md:
Up to a scalar, $D$ is a sub-sum of the original microscopic local terms,
so its interaction strength per site is still at most one. Write
$\operatorname{ad}_A(B):=[A,B]=AB-BA$ and
$\operatorname{ad}_A^0(B):=B$. If $O_Z$ is supported on at most $k$ sites, then
\begin{align}
 \|\operatorname{ad}_D^r(O_Z)\|
 \le(2k)^r r!\,\|O_Z\|,\qquad r\ge0.
 \label{app:eq:microscopic-commutator}
\end{align}
Indeed, after $j$ nonzero commutators the support has at most
$k+j(k-1)$ sites. The sum of the norms of terms that can contribute to the
next commutator is at most $k+j(k-1)\le k(j+1)$. Summing over ordered
sequences of local terms and using $\|[X,Y]\|\le2\|X\|\|Y\|$ yields
$\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}2k(j+1)=(2k)^rr!$.
Applying this estimate term by term to $B$ gives, for $0\le s\le s_0$,
\begin{align}
 \|e^{sD}Be^{-sD}\|
 \le\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{s^r}{r!}
                  \|\operatorname{ad}_D^r(B)\|
 \le\frac{b_\partial}{1-2ks}\le2b_\partial.
 \label{app:eq:conjugated-boundary}
\end{align}
Let $F(s)=e^{sD}e^{-s(D+B)}$. Differentiation gives
$F'(s)=-(e^{sD}Be^{-sD})F(s)$ and $F(0)=I$, so the integral equation and
Gronwall's inequality imply $\|F(s)\|\le e^{2b_\partial s}$.
Since $e^{sD}\Omega=e^{se_0}F(s)\Omega$, the first bound in
\eqref{app:eq:moment} follows. The spectral theorem gives the second.
The argument uses microscopic sites rather than treating an entire layer
as one site; in particular, $s_0$ has no dependence on $\mathcal A$,
$\ell$, or $n$.

label: app:lem:variational
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Variational projection lemma

label: app:eq:minmax
title: Proof
body_md:
Use $P\Omega/\|P\Omega\|$ as a trial state. For a restriction to a
subspace, the min--max principle gives
\begin{align}
 \lambda_1(G_P)=
 \min_{\substack{U\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}P\\\dim U=2}}
 \max_{\substack{u\in U\\\|u\|=1}}\langle u|G|u\rangle
 \ge\lambda_1(G)=\Delta.
 \label{app:eq:minmax}
\end{align}
This proves uniqueness and the gap estimate. Since
$G\ge\Delta(I-|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|)$,
$1-|\langle\Omega|\Omega_P\rangle|^2\le e_P/\Delta$.
For phase-aligned unit vectors, the squared distance is at most twice
this quantity.
head: environment

label: app:lem:cutcount
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Cut count for an absolutely convergent series

label: app:eq:total-cost
title: Proof
body_md:
First consider a polynomial of total degree at most $Q$.
Organize the $\ell$ cuts into a binary tree, splitting each set into
children whose cardinalities differ by at most one. For a monomial
$\lambda^q$, compare the \emph{total} costs of the two children $I,J$:
\begin{align}
 d_{I,J}(q):=\sum_{s\in I}q_s-\sum_{s\in J}q_s.
 \label{app:eq:total-cost}
\end{align}
Choose $I$ if $d_{I,J}\le0$ and $J$ otherwise. This tie convention gives
every monomial a unique leaf. The selected cost is at most half the parent
cost at each step. A leaf depth $h$ lies between
$\lfloor\log_2\ell\rfloor$ and $\lceil\log_2\ell\rceil$, so its selected
cut satisfies $q_s\le Q2^{-h}\le2Q/\ell$, and thus $q_s\le p_*$.

Let $N_F=2Q+1$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/N_F}$.
The selection functions $\chi_L(d)=\mathbf1_{d\le0}$ and
$\chi_R(d)=\mathbf1_{d>0}$ have the exact discrete Fourier representations
on $-Q\le d\le Q$
\begin{align}
 \chi_b(d)=\sum_{r=0}^{N_F-1}\widehat\chi_b(r)\omega^{rd},
 \qquad
 \widehat\chi_b(r)=\frac1{N_F}\sum_{a=-Q}^Q\chi_b(a)\omega^{-ra},
 \qquad |\widehat\chi_b(r)|\le1.
 \label{app:eq:selection-fourier}
\end{align}
Every coefficient of $q_s$ in $d_{I,J}$ is $0,1$, or $-1$.
Consequently, $\omega^{r d_{I,J}(q)}$ is implemented by multiplying the
variables by unit phases. Multiply the selection functions along a path,
and at its leaf retain only powers at most $p_*$. The assigned monomial
survives exactly once; all other paths cancel in the Fourier sums.
There are at most $N_F^{\lceil\log_2\ell\rceil}$ phase terms per leaf.
Their coefficients are products of the Fourier coefficients and have
modulus at most one. This proves the identity and the branch count for
polynomials. Repeated phase values are kept as separate indexed terms.

For the full series, split $F=F_{\le Q}+F_{>Q}$, and denote the branch
operation by $\mathscr S$. Absolute convergence allows rearrangement.
One branch's leaf-degree truncation retains any monomial at most once,
so
\begin{align}
 \|F_{>Q}(\mathbf1)\|\le\delta_Q(F),\qquad
 \|\mathscr S F_{>Q}\|\le N_{\mathrm{ph}}\delta_Q(F).
 \label{app:eq:cutcount-tail}
\end{align}
Take $R_Q=F_{>Q}(\mathbf1)-\mathscr S F_{>Q}$.
There is no additional factor $p_*+1$ in this tail estimate.

label: app:lem:poincare
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Row Poincar\'e estimate

label: app:eq:path-poincare-proof
title: Proof
body_md:
Telescoping along each random path and applying Cauchy--Schwarz yields
\begin{align}
 \operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)
 &\le\sum_w\pi(w)|f(w)-f(a)|^2\notag\\
 &\le\sum_w\pi(w)\,
       \mathbb E\!\left[|\gamma_w|\sum_{e\in\gamma_w}|\nabla_e f|^2\right]
 \le b^2\sum_eG_e|\nabla_e f|^2
 \le8b^3\mathcal E(f,f).
 \label{app:eq:path-poincare-proof}
\end{align}
The spectral statement follows from the unitary identification between
$L^2(\pi)$ and the row Hilbert space by multiplication by $\sqrt\pi$.

label: app:lem:history
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Exact history representation and Bell extraction

title: Proof
body_md:
Particles exchange only with vacancies, so their order is preserved.
A central $VV\to\Phi_P$ rewrite adds a pair at the innermost positions
on both sides; its inverse removes that same pair. Both tagged particles
can return to the central bond only after all ordinary pairs have been
removed. Thus each applicable rewrite maps a history vector to the
corresponding adjacent history vector without changing the Bell pairing.
For an interior exchange the amplitude ratio is one, for extension it is
$1/\sqrt2$, and for the first root edge it is $1/\sqrt b$.
These are exactly $\sqrt{\mu(y)/\mu(x)}$ in
\eqref{app:eq:row-Laplacian}, including the diagonal coefficients of each
normalized edge projector. Summing the edge identities proves
\eqref{app:eq:intertwining} and invariance of the history space.

One can also track formal labels by writing the root as
$A_bA_{b-1}\cdots A_1B_1B_2\cdots B_b$ and preserving order within
each species. An adjacent pair $A_i,B_j$ meets at bond $b-i+j$, counted
from the left. It is at the central bond precisely when $i=j$.
This is a mathematical labeling argument, not an enlargement of the
physical alphabet.

For $w\in F_m$, the outermost $m$ particles on each side always carry the
same $m$ Bell pairs. On each half-row, coherently retain the occupation
pattern and move these ordered color registers into fixed output
registers. This operation is an isometry on the target subspace and can
be extended by unused output space. The remaining occupation and color
registers retain orthogonality between different patterns. The same
isometries work for every $w$, so the common $m$-pair factor also separates
from an arbitrary superposition, giving \eqref{app:eq:row-Bell-factor}.
This statement is about vectors in the initialized history space, not
arbitrary physical states with sufficiently many particles. The
isometries are local across $L|R$; no bound on their circuit depth inside
either half is asserted.
head: environment

label: app:lem:well
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Rank-one well with an illegal-sector penalty

title: Proof
body_md:
On the legal subspace, $H_{\mathrm{raw}}$ is a rank-one negative
perturbation of a positive operator. It has at most one negative
eigenvalue: a two-dimensional negative spectral subspace would contain
a nonzero vector orthogonal to $o$, whose expectation of
$J_{\mathrm{phys}}-|o\rangle\langle o|$ is nonnegative, a contradiction.
The root trial state has energy $r_o-1\le-1/2$, so a negative eigenvalue
exists and is simple. Since $H_{\mathrm{raw}}\ge-I$ on the legal space,
$\lambda_*\le1$. On the illegal space,
$J_{\mathrm{phys}}+2\Gamma-R_o\ge I$.
Every other eigenvalue on the full space is therefore nonnegative,
proving the gap assertion. Taking the ground-state expectation gives
$\lambda_*=|\langle o|\Omega\rangle|^2-
\langle\Omega|J_{\mathrm{phys}}|\Omega\rangle
\le|\langle o|\Omega\rangle|^2$.
Finally, on the legal orthogonal complement of an invariant history
space containing $o$, the well vanishes and the Hamiltonian is
nonnegative. Thus the negative eigenstate lies in the history space.
head: environment

label: app:lem:startup
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Startup amplitude

title: Proof
body_md:
Use the Dyson expansion around the block-diagonal part
$\bigoplus_t(K_t+W_t)$. Its interaction term has nonnegative off-diagonal
blocks in the expansion of $e^{-t_0\widehat J}$.
Retain only trajectories with exactly the $M$ forward activations
$0\to1\to\cdots\to M$ at times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_M<t_0$.
Each contributes a factor $1/2$. Equation~\eqref{app:eq:killed-comparison}
bounds the combined diagonal activation cost below by $e^{-t_0}$.
After its birth at $t_j$, row $j$ evolves independently for time
$t_0-t_j$; its final return amplitude is at least $p$ by
\eqref{app:eq:return-kernel}. Their product is at least $p^M$.
Integrating over the activation simplex gives its volume $t_0^M/M!$.
At $t_0=M$, use $M^M/M!\ge1$.
Importantly, rows are allowed to move during startup; they are not
required to remain frozen at the source.

label: app:lem:resolvent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{app:lem:resolvent}
Let $J$ be a real symmetric matrix on a finite set of at least two
vertices, with $J_{xy}\le0$ for $x\ne y$ and connected off-diagonal
graph. Suppose $\pi(x)>0$, $\sum_x\pi(x)=1$, and $J\sqrt\pi=0$.
Let $\tau$ be the best Poincar\'e constant of the associated Doob chain.
For a source $a$ and target $F$, write $p=\pi(a)>0$, $q=\pi(F)>0$, and
$|v_F\rangle=q^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in F}\sqrt{\pi(x)}|x\rangle$.
For every $s>0$,
\begin{align}
 s\langle v_F|(J+sI)^{-1}|a\rangle
 \ge\sqrt{pq}\,
    \exp\!\left[-(p^{-1/2}+q^{-1/2})\sqrt{s\tau}\right].
 \label{app:eq:resolvent-lemma}
\end{align}

label: app:prop:adiabatic-path
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Uniformly gapped product-state path

label: app:eq:path-trial
title: Proof
body_md:
Every term preserves the legal subspace and its orthogonal complement.
On the legal subspace, $\Gamma=0$ and $R_o=|o\rangle\langle o|$.
Consequently, $g_*H(s)$ restricts to
$sJ_{\rm phys}-|o\rangle\langle o|$. A rank-one negative perturbation
of a positive operator has at most one negative eigenvalue. The root
trial state has expectation
\begin{align}
 \langle o|g_*H(s)|o\rangle=sr_o-1\le-\tfrac12.
 \label{app:eq:path-trial}
\end{align}
Thus a simple negative eigenvalue $-\lambda(s)$ exists, and
$1-sr_o\le\lambda(s)\le1$. All other legal eigenvalues are
nonnegative. On the illegal subspace,
\begin{align}
 sJ_{\rm phys}+2\Gamma-R_o\ge2I-I=I.
 \label{app:eq:path-illegal}
\end{align}
The ground state is therefore unique on the full physical space, and its
gap is at least $\lambda(s)/g_*$. At $s=0$ its ground vector is exactly
$o$. At $s=1$ it is the previously constructed state. This is the
rank-one argument of Appendix~\ref{app:row-gap}, applied for every $s$;
it never requires a lower bound on the internal propagation gap.

Multiplying positive propagation terms by $s\in[0,1]$ cannot increase
any local norm. The derivative is $J_{\rm phys}/g_*$, with the same
finite supports and uniformly bounded interaction strength. Increase
the one fixed $g_*$, if necessary, to bound both strengths by one.
Finite-dimensional spectral perturbation theory gives a smooth choice
of the unique ground-state projector along this linear path. The same
argument holds after serpentine re-embedding, since the embedding does
not depend on $s$.
head: environment
name: Proof of the path and gap assertions

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply the entangling-rate and exact quasi-adiabatic-continuation
results of Refs.~\cite{PhysRevB.72.045141,PhysRevLett.111.170501,Marien2016}.
For exact spectral transport and its uniform quasi-locality we use the
finite-volume spectral-flow estimates of
Ref.~\cite{Bachmann2012Automorphic}, in particular Proposition~2.4 and
Theorem~4.8. The local propagation estimates are of Lieb--Robinson
type~\cite{ref:Nachtergaele2006-LR}.
Here it is important to check uniformity even though some microscopic
couplings depend on the chosen finite size. The path has a common gap
lower bound, common finite interaction range, bounded local dimension,
and uniform local bounds for both $H(s)$ and $\partial_sH(s)$.
These are precisely the inputs to a uniform Lieb--Robinson bound and
to a uniform exact spectral-flow filter. No translation invariance or
lower bound on each nonzero coupling is needed for the resulting
finite-volume estimates.

For clarity, the geometric summation underlying the application is as
follows. The ground states can be transported by a unitary generated
by a quasi-local Hermitian operator $\mathcal G(s)$ with a decomposition
\begin{align}
 \mathcal G(s)=\sum_{i\in\Lambda}\sum_{r\ge1}g_{i,r}(s),\qquad
 \operatorname{supp}g_{i,r}(s)\subseteq B(i,c r),\qquad
 \sup_s\|g_{i,r}(s)\|\le C_N(1+r)^{-N}.
 \label{app:eq:path-quasilocal}
\end{align}
For every fixed $N$, the constants $c,C_N$ depend only on the uniform
local data and gap, not on the volume. This is the standard
quasi-local decomposition of exact spectral flow. Terms supported
entirely on one side of the cut do not change its entanglement.
A radius-$cr$ ball contains $O(r^\nu)$ sites, and at most
$O(\mathcal A r)$ centers have such a ball crossing a planar cut.
The small-incremental-entangling bound (Theorem~3 of
Ref.~\cite{Marien2016}) controls each crossing term by
its norm times the logarithm of its supported Hilbert-space dimension,
independently of the remaining sites treated as ancillas. Hence the
integrated entangling-rate bound gives
\begin{align}
 |S_1(\Omega(s))-S_1(\Omega(0))|
 \le C\mathcal A\log6\int_0^s
       \sum_{r\ge1}r^{\nu+1}C_N(1+r)^{-N}\,du
 \le C_\nu\mathcal A
 \label{app:eq:path-rate-integral}
\end{align}
for any fixed $N>\nu+2$. The integrated form also covers points at
which a reduced density matrix has zero eigenvalues. Finally,
$S_1(\Omega(0))=0$ because $o$ is a product state.
This explicitly verifies the finite-size-uniform area-law stability
argument for the present rectangular geometries.

label: app:cor:adiabatic-separation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{app:cor:adiabatic-separation}
For each fixed $0<\alpha<1$ in two dimensions, the aspect-ratio choice
of Corollary~\ref{app:cor:renyi} gives, on the same family,
\begin{align}
 S_1(\Omega)=O(\mathcal A),\qquad
 S_\alpha(\Omega)\ge c_\alpha n.
 \label{app:eq:adiabatic-separation}
\end{align}
Here $c_\alpha>0$ is independent of $n$, and the inequalities hold
for sufficiently large systems at the fixed $\alpha$.
For every fixed $\nu\ge3$, one and the same hypercubic family has this
separation for every fixed $0<\alpha<1$. All these families have the
uniformly gapped product-state paths of
Proposition~\ref{app:prop:adiabatic-path}. In particular, their
$S_\alpha$ also obey an area law for $\alpha\ge1$ by monotonicity.

Corollary~\ref{app:cor:renyi}. The entropy-index-dependent choice in two
dimensions changes the aspect ratio, not the uniform path estimates.
In dimensions at least three no such choice is needed. For

label: app:thm:thermal-transfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{app:thm:thermal-transfer}
There are constants $C,\Delta_0>0$, independent of $m,\beta,\alpha$,
such that, for every $m\ge3$ and $0<\alpha<1$,
\begin{align}
 \beta\Delta_0\ge32m\log6+Cm^{3/2}+\log16
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 E_{p,\alpha}(\rho_{\beta,m})
 \ge m\log2-\log2-\kappa_\alpha(Cm^{3/2}+\log8).
 \label{app:eq:thermal-1d-finite}
\end{align}
The row has $n=32m$ sites, on-site dimension at most six, and physical
gap at least $\Delta_0$. Its local data and gap bound are uniform in
$m$. The lower bound applies to every purification in
\eqref{app:eq:thermal-Ep-def}.
head: environment
name: One-dimensional finite-temperature transfer

label: app:lem:near-pure
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Transfer of a Schmidt tail to every purification

label: app:eq:purification-tail
title: Proof
body_md:
For any purification $\Psi\in LL'RR'$, define the normalized ancillary
vector $\eta$ by
$(\langle\Omega|\otimes I)|\Psi\rangle=\sqrt{1-\delta}\,|\eta\rangle$.
Then $\|\Psi-\Omega\otimes\eta\|=d_\delta$, and $\eta$ may itself be
entangled across $L'|R'$. If $p_i,q_j$ are the Schmidt probabilities of
$\Omega,\eta$, those of $\Omega\otimes\eta$ are $p_iq_j$. The sum of
any $R$ of these products is at most the sum of the $R$ largest $p_i$:
group the selected pairs by $i$ and use $\sum_jq_j=1$.
Hence $T_{\Omega\otimes\eta}(R)\ge T_\Omega(R)$. Distance to the set
of vectors of Schmidt rank at most $R$ is $1$-Lipschitz, giving
\begin{align}
 T_\Psi(R)\ge
       \left(\sqrt{T_\Omega(R)}-d_\delta\right)_+^2.
 \label{app:eq:purification-tail}
\end{align}
For Schmidt probabilities $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots$, put
$M_\alpha=\sum_js_j^\alpha$. Then
\begin{align}
 s_{R+1}\le(M_\alpha/R)^{1/\alpha},\qquad
 T(R)\le s_{R+1}^{1-\alpha}\sum_{j>R}s_j^\alpha
       \le M_\alpha^{1/\alpha}R^{-(1-\alpha)/\alpha}.
 \label{app:eq:tail-to-entropy}
\end{align}
Thus $S_\alpha\ge\log R+\kappa_\alpha\log T(R)$.
Apply this to \eqref{app:eq:purification-tail} and take the infimum
over all purifications and ancillary bipartitions.

label: app:cor:thermal-1d
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Joint one-dimensional thermal lower bound

label: app:eq:thermal-1d-zeta
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\kappa=\kappa_\alpha$ and
$R_0=\min\{\beta^{2/3},\kappa^{-2}\}$. Choose $0<\zeta<1$ such that
\begin{align}
 32\zeta\log6+C\zeta^{3/2}\le\Delta_0/2,
 \qquad C\sqrt\zeta\le\log2/4.
 \label{app:eq:thermal-1d-zeta}
\end{align}
Set $m=\lfloor\zeta R_0\rfloor$. Increase $\beta_0\ge1$ and decrease
$\alpha_0$ so that $\zeta R_0\ge32$, $\kappa\le1$, and
$\beta\Delta_0/2\ge\log16$ throughout the stated range.
Then $m\ge16$, $m\ge\zeta R_0/2$, and $m\le\zeta\beta^{2/3}$;
the first inequality in \eqref{app:eq:thermal-1d-zeta} gives the
cooling condition in \eqref{app:eq:thermal-1d-finite}.
Also $\kappa\sqrt m\le\sqrt\zeta$, so
$\kappa Cm^{3/2}\le m\log2/4$ and
$\log2+\kappa\log8\le4\log2\le m\log2/4$.
Theorem~\ref{app:thm:thermal-transfer} yields
$E_{p,\alpha}\ge\tfrac12m\log2\ge\tfrac14\zeta\log2\,R_0$.
For $\alpha=a\beta^{-1/3}$ with sufficiently small fixed $a$,
$R_0=\Theta(\beta^{2/3})$. Placing the entire purifying ancilla on the
right gives the dimension upper bound
$E_{p,\alpha}\le\log\dim\mathcal H_L=16m\log6$, proving
\eqref{app:eq:thermal-1d-diagonal} on the selected family.

label: app:prop:gibbs-compression
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Joint temperature--accuracy lower bound in one dimension

label: app:eq:gibbs-ground-distance
title: Proof
head: environment
